clinicalPearls: Plague is a systemic zoonosis caused by Yersinia pestis, predominantly affecting small rodents in rural areas of Africa, Asia, and the Americas and usually transmitted to humans by an arthropod (flea) vector; less often via contact with animal tissues or respiratory droplets (p.1341).

Three principal clinical forms: bubonic, septicemic, and pneumonic. Worldwide, bubonic plague is the predominant reported form; a minority (10-20%) present as primary septicemic or pneumonic disease (p.1343).

Bubonic plague: after a 2-6 day incubation, sudden onset of fever (>38 degC), malaise, myalgia, dizziness, and increasing pain from progressive regional lymphadenitis. The bubo is a tense, tender swelling with a boggy consistency and underlying hard core, usually solitary and erythematous with periganglionic edema, most commonly inguinal but may be crural, axillary, cervical, or submaxillary depending on bite site (p.1343).
Children most commonly present with cervical or axillary buboes; abdominal pain from intraabdominal node involvement can occur without other visible signs (p.1343).

Primary pneumonic plague follows inhalation of infectious droplets from another person or animal with plague pneumonia; short incubation (a few hours to 2-3 days, range 1-7 days) with abrupt fever, headache, myalgia, weakness, nausea, vomiting, dizziness; respiratory signs (cough, dyspnea, chest pain, sputum with hemoptysis) typically appear after 24 h (p.1344).

Primary pneumonic plague is generally the least common but most fatal of the main presentations; treated pneumonic plague has an estimated death rate of about 17% versus 98% for untreated pneumonic plague (p.1343).

Primary septicemic plague (10-25% of infections) presents as gram-negative septicemia (hypotension, shock) WITHOUT preceding lymphadenopathy; occurs in all age groups but risk is elevated in persons over 40 (p.1344).

WBC count is generally raised (10,000-20,000/uL) with neutrophilic leukocytosis and left shift; counts can be very high in children (>100,000/uL), but in some cases the WBC is normal or leukopenia develops. DIC occurs in a significant minority (p.1346).
Appropriate treatment of bubonic plague resolves fever within 2-5 days, but buboes may remain enlarged for more than a week after initial treatment and can become fluctuant (p.1344).
harrison.pathophysiology: Y. pestis is a gram-negative bacterium of the order Enterobacterales that recently evolved from the enteric pathogen Y. pseudotuberculosis. It has a two-stage life cycle alternating between arthropod (flea) and a wide range of mammalian hosts. In the flea, the organism multiplies and forms biofilm-embedded aggregates in the midgut; some fleas become 'blocked' at the proventriculus and regurgitate bacteria into the bite site, while early-phase unblocked transmission also occurs. In the mammalian host, dissemination from the inoculation site is initially dependent on plasminogen activator (Pla), which activates plasminogen, degrades complement, and binds laminin, and is essential for high-level virulence and bubo formation. Bacteria are rapidly transported to regional lymph nodes where Y. pestis replicates extracellularly with full expression of antiphagocytic systems (type III secretion machinery and effectors encoded by pYV plus the F1 capsule), producing a bubo (hemorrhagic/necrotic node with thrombosed vessels, replaced architecture, and abundant bacteria). LcrV targets phagocytes and exerts an anti-inflammatory effect, and modified lipopolysaccharide minimizes Toll-like receptor 4 stimulation, prolonging high-grade bacteremia. Spread via efferent lymphatics to the thoracic duct produces high-grade bacteremia and hematogenous seeding of spleen, liver, secondary buboes, lungs (secondary plague pneumonia), and meninges, with uncontrolled septicemia leading to death; the septicemic phase can occur without an obvious prior bubo (p.1342-1343).
additionalDifferentials: Acute focal lymphadenopathy of other etiologies (for bubonic plague): streptococcal or staphylococcal infection, tularemia, cat-scratch disease, tick typhus, infectious mononucleosis, lymphatic filariasis (p.1343).
Tuberculosis (in differential of fever and hemoptysis in plague-endemic areas, as a small-airborne-particle-transmitted infection) (p.1347).
Tonsillitis with peritonsillar abscess (resembles plague pharyngitis) (p.1344).
additionalInvestigations: Bubo aspirate (bubonic), bronchoalveolar lavage fluid or sputum (pneumonic), and blood (septicemic) are the appropriate specimens; culture of postmortem organ biopsy can also be diagnostic. Transport medium such as Cary-Blair preserves viability (p.1345).

Direct microscopy: Gram-negative coccobacilli with characteristic bipolar 'closed safety pin' appearance on Wayson or Wright-Giemsa stain; bipolar bacilli may be visible on direct blood smear in septicemic plague, indicating very high circulating bacterial numbers and a poor prognosis (p.1345).

Culture on nutrient-rich media (sheep blood agar, brain-heart infusion broth) and selective agar (MacConkey, EMB, or Yersinia-specific CIN agar); optimal growth at <37 degC (25-29 degC). Y. pestis is oxidase-negative, catalase-positive, urease-negative, indole-negative, lactose-negative, and nonmotile (distinguishing it from other Yersinia species) (p.1345).

F1 antigen detection: direct immunofluorescence and rapid immunochromatographic test strip (F1RDT), effective on bubo aspirates and sputum and widely used in endemic countries; a Pla antigen strip can detect F1-negative strains (p.1345).
PCR/RT-PCR requiring positivity for at least two Y. pestis-specific targets (e.g., caf1, pla, and chromosomal genes); FDA-authorized BioFire FilmArray panels include Y. pestis (p.1346).
Serology: rising hemagglutinating antibody titer to F1 antigen, or seroconversion/fourfold rise in paired sera; ELISA for IgG and IgM to F1 antigen (p.1345-1346).
WHO case definitions (suspected/probable/confirmed) guide presumptive diagnosis followed by reference laboratory confirmation (p.1345).
redFlags: Pneumonic plague is transmissible person-to-person via respiratory droplets (productive cough), making it a public-health emergency requiring immediate isolation and notification (p.1344, 1347).

Aerosolized Y. pestis is a recognized potential bioterrorism agent (Tier 1 select agent); an outbreak of primary pneumonic plague in a nonendemic region or urban setting should raise concern for intentional release (p.1342, 1344, 1345).
Rapid progression of primary pneumonic plague from segmental pneumonitis to lobar and bilateral involvement with hemoptysis and ARDS within hours to days (p.1344).
Bipolar bacilli visible on direct blood smear indicate very high circulating bacterial numbers and a poor prognosis (p.1345).
Disseminated intravascular coagulation with shock in septicemic disease (p.1346).
harrison.prognosis: Untreated plague carries high mortality, but it is treatable with antimicrobials. Treated pneumonic plague has an estimated death rate of about 17% compared with 98% for untreated pneumonic plague. In the United States, case-fatality fell from 66% in 1900-1941 to 16% in the post-antibiotic era (1942 onward); in 2000-2018, mortality was 8% in patients receiving any antimicrobial and 4% in those receiving currently recommended high-efficacy agents. The global case-fatality rate notified to WHO for 2013-2018 was 17%. Visible bipolar bacilli on direct blood smear signal very high bacteremia and poor prognosis (p.1343, 1345).
pitfalls: The term 'septicemic plague' can be confusing because most patients with buboes have detectable bacteremia at some stage, with or without systemic sepsis signs (p.1344).
Automated biochemical or mass-spectrometry identification systems can misidentify Y. pestis as Y. pseudotuberculosis or other species (p.1345).
Meningeal plague may be associated with suboptimal antimicrobial therapy (delayed treatment, penicillin use, or low-dose tetracycline) (p.1344).

A single negative rapid antigen test is insufficient to exclude plague; WHO exclusion requires two negative F1RDT tests on specimens collected 24 h apart when confirmatory tests are unavailable (p.1345-1346).

F1RDT specificity for culture-confirmed pneumonic plague was only 71%, so a positive sputum test in an endemic area identifies a probable case requiring treatment but needs additional confirmatory testing (p.1345-1346).
Culture yield can be low after prehospital antimicrobial use (as observed in the 2017 Madagascar outbreak) (p.1345).
harrison.severityClassification: WHO case classification of plague: Suspected case (clinical presentation suggestive of plague plus an epidemiologic context of possible exposure within 10 days of onset); Probable case (suspected case plus one of: F1 antigen detected by rapid test or immunofluorescence, a single anti-F1 serology without prior infection/immunization, or direct microscopy showing bipolar-staining gram-negative coccobacilli); Confirmed case (suspected case plus one of: isolation of Y. pestis, seroconversion or fourfold anti-F1 titer change in paired sera, or species-specific PCR positivity); Not a case (suspected case with negative confirmatory testing) (p.1345).

Salam AP et al: Deaths associated with pneumonic plague, 1946-2017
management: Prompt antimicrobial therapy with an aminoglycoside such as streptomycin or gentamicin as first-line treatment
Alternative or adjunctive antimicrobials such as fluoroquinolones or tetracyclines including doxycycline, with chloramphenicol for plague meningitis
Supportive care for sepsis including intravenous fluids, oxygen and organ support in critical illness
Respiratory droplet isolation of patients with pneumonic plague until adequately treated
Post-exposure antibiotic prophylaxis with doxycycline or a fluoroquinolone for close contacts of pneumonic cases
Urgent notification to public health authorities with contact tracing
Environmental flea and rodent control to interrupt transmission
Escalation to critical care for septicaemic or pneumonic disease with monitoring for complications
